eac1bbb069:
__init__ sets up a fresh instance. It runs after the object already exists, so it is an initializer, not a constructor. The real constructor is __new__, which allocates the object. You almost never touch __new__. It has two legitimate uses:

  • subclassing immutable types, like int or tuple, where the value must exist before __init__ runs;
  • controlling how many instances exist (singletons, caches).
c96926cd56: The full lifecycle has three hooks. __new__ allocates, __init__ initializes, __del__ finalizes. You will write __init__ constantly, __new__ almost never, and __del__ almost never. But you need to understand __del__, because its caveats bite.
e0efc22923:
Three caveats make __del__ unreliable for real cleanup. First, it is not guaranteed to run at interpreter shutdown. Modules may already be torn down when it fires. Second, exceptions raised inside __del__ are swallowed (printed to stderr, then ignored), so a failing finalizer fails silently. Third, the prompt teardown you see above is CPython's reference counting, an implementation detail. Other implementations collect later. Since PEP 442 the cyclic collector can reclaim cycles that define __del__, but you still cannot count on when.

The practical rule: never put essential cleanup in __del__. Files, locks, and transactions belong in context managers (section 6). Use __del__ only for best-effort logging or releasing purely internal resources.
769022e4b8: A class offers three kinds of methods. An instance method takes self and works on one object's data. This is the default, and most methods are instance methods. A class method takes cls (the class itself) instead of an instance. Its main job is alternate construction: factories that build objects in a convenient way. A static method takes neither. It is a plain function that lives in the class's namespace for organization.
32721a583e: The mental model: a property is an object that lives on the class, and it intercepts attribute access on instances. Assigning p.price_cents = 1499 does not write into the instance dictionary. The property's setter runs instead. Leave off the setter and you get a read-only attribute for free. This also explains a subtle rule. Because the property lives on the class, it works the same for every instance. A subclass can override just the getter or just the setter.
d287ae2fe0: A single leading underscore, _balance, means "internal, don't touch" by convention only. The language enforces nothing. Other code can read and write it freely. The convention is still worth following. It marks the boundary between your class's public contract and its implementation details. Tools like linters and IDEs also treat _names as internal.
fccc1239bb: The Savings example shows the feature working as designed. The subclass's __balance becomes _Savings__balance, so it never overwrites the base class's _Account__balance. Without mangling, the subclass assignment would have silently replaced the account's numeric balance with the string "separate". Then total() would have broken in a confusing way.
1a5f22cdf6: Use mangling when you write a base class whose internals must survive subclassing by code you don't control. That mostly means framework and library code. In application code, a single underscore plus discipline is enough. And never treat mangling as security: anyone can read _Account__balance. Privacy in Python is a social contract, documented in names.
b95745d414:
The checkout function is the important part. It never checks which subclass it received. It calls total() and trusts the contract. That trust has a name: the Liskov substitution principle. In plain terms, a subclass must be usable anywhere its base class is expected.

The practical version: don't break the promises the base class makes. If Price.total() never returns a negative number, no subclass's total() may return one either. If the base __init__ accepts cents, a subclass shouldn't demand a completely different signature from code that constructs prices generically. Inheritance gives you reuse; the price of reuse is honoring the contract.
907857dc8a: OrderList shows the composition-vs-inheritance smell in miniature. Inheriting from list gives you append, sort, slicing, and dozens of other methods. Most of them make no sense on an order and can corrupt its invariants. The order can't stop someone from calling bad.sort() or bad.clear(). With composition, Order exposes exactly the operations it wants: add and total. The list stays an implementation detail.
1043124a27: Choosing between them: use inheritance when the relationship is genuinely is-a and you want substitutability. Code written against the base should accept the subclass. Use composition when one object uses another, when you only want part of another class's behavior, or when you're unsure. Composition couples less: changing the held object doesn't ripple through a hierarchy. A common failure mode is inheriting for code reuse alone ("I want list's methods"). That buys reuse at the cost of a contract you never meant to sign.
009083da3d:
A class can inherit from more than one base: class Child(Left, Right). When you call a method, Python searches the bases in a well-defined order called the method resolution order (MRO). For the diamond below, Child inherits from Left and Right, which both inherit from Base. The MRO is Child → Left → Right → Base → object. Python computes it with the C3 linearization algorithm. You don't need the algorithm's internals. The conceptual rules are:

  • a class always comes before its parents;
  • parents appear left-to-right in the order listed;
  • each class appears exactly once.
9ba1c0bbca:
Sometimes several bases each need their own constructor arguments. Then every __init__ takes only the arguments it owns and forwards the rest with **kwargs. Each one calls super().__init__(**kwargs) so the next class in the MRO gets its turn. Three rules keep the chain intact:

  • use keyword-only arguments;
  • accept and forward **kwargs in every __init__ in the chain;
  • never skip the super().__init__() call.
ae7dac00e4: Trace it: Item(...) has no __init__, so Priced.__init__ runs first (MRO order). It takes cents, forwards sku and qty. Stocked.__init__ takes qty, forwards sku. Base.__init__ takes sku, forwards nothing to object.__init__. Every class initialized exactly the piece it owns. Base appears once in the MRO, so sku is set once. No double initialization: that is the classic diamond bug this pattern prevents.
9951786901:
An ABC can also provide concrete methods — shared behavior that subclasses inherit — alongside the abstract ones. Use an ABC when you own the hierarchy and want three things:

  • a compile-time-style guarantee that subclasses implement the contract;
  • isinstance checks that mean something;
  • a place for shared base behavior.

The cost is coupling. Every implementer must inherit from your class, which is awkward across library boundaries.
2f0ef71ca7:
Choosing between them: reach for an ABC when you are building a family of classes you own and want enforcement plus shared code. Reach for a Protocol when you are describing a capability that unrelated classes may already have, especially across module or library boundaries. A Protocol is also the lighter annotation for function parameters. "I need something with a total() method" says exactly what the function needs, nothing more.

One caveat on runtime_checkable: it only verifies that the methods exist. It will not catch a total() that takes the wrong arguments. Static type checkers verify the full signature; runtime checks do not.
65607ed49d: The __eq__ returning NotImplemented deserves a callout. Say you compare a LineItem to a string. Returning NotImplemented tells Python "I don't know how to compare these — ask the other side". Python then tries the string's reflected comparison. If that also declines, it falls back to identity. Returning False instead would be subtly wrong: it claims the comparison was meaningful and answered no.
c8a0027a05: The with statement exists for setup/teardown pairs: open/close, begin/commit, lock/unlock. __enter__ runs on entry, and its return value binds to the as target. __exit__ runs on exit, including when the block raises. It receives the exception type, value, and traceback (all None when nothing went wrong).
e37492e26c: The second block shows the guarantee that makes context managers essential. __exit__ ran during the exception and printed the rollback. Because it returned False, the exception continued to the caller. Returning True would swallow it. Do that only when swallowing is the documented purpose (like contextlib.suppress). This is also why __del__ is the wrong tool for cleanup. A context manager's teardown is deterministic and exception-aware; a finalizer's is neither.
d49dd77bf0: The trap: defining __eq__ in a class sets __hash__ to None. The language does this deliberately. A hand-written __eq__ usually means value semantics, and the old identity hash would then be wrong. So Python disables hashing rather than let it be silently inconsistent. The result surprises everyone once:
a5f6d4a74e: When to use __slots__: many instances of a small, stable class — points, rows, tokens, AST nodes — where profiling shows attribute dictionaries eating real memory. When to avoid it: everywhere else. For ordinary application classes the savings are unmeasurable and the rigidity is real. __slots__ is a memory optimization, not a design tool. It doesn't make a class "tighter" or "cleaner". It makes it cheaper and less flexible.
18d01fa788: Smell 3: an abstraction with one implementation. An ABC with a single concrete subclass, a strategy pattern with one strategy, an interface implemented exactly once. The abstraction promises flexibility that nobody uses, while every reader pays the indirection cost. Write the concrete thing first. Extract the abstraction when the second implementation actually arrives. That moment is obvious, and the abstraction will fit better for having waited.
c417f13ed2: Each pair produces identical behavior. The right-hand version is shorter, has fewer moving parts, and leaves a clear seam for growing later. That is the general principle behind all three. Add structure in response to real pressure, not in anticipation of it. Real pressure means a second implementation, a second role, a genuinely shared contract.
